reading.body:
Government AI activity is now a matter of public record: federal agencies disclose what they run, GAO audits those inventories, and 2,425 state AI bills are tracked to their source.

The pattern is layered oversight. GAO reviews federal AI inventories and management, state legislation is tracked bill by bill, and international indexes from Oxford Insights, OECD.AI, and Stanford HAI compare national readiness, strategies, and policy execution. This makes government AI adoption measurable and auditable, which shapes where and how public-sector systems can operate.

What this record does not show is the physical layer. The Oxford Insights index scores infrastructure as one dimension, but no scores or infrastructure findings appear here. The data covers governance, law, and policy, not the compute, buildings, or power behind the systems being governed.

summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The most concrete measured picture of government AI comes from the U.S. GAO, which reviewed implementation at major federal agencies. GAO found that 20 of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, described as specific challenges or opportunities that AI may solve, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. Most of those reported use cases were still in the planning phase rather than in production, and in about 200 instances agencies reported that they were currently using AI. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of use cases.

GAO also documented serious weaknesses in the underlying data. Its analysis of agency inventories found instances of incomplete and inaccurate information, with five agencies providing comprehensive information for each reported use case while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data. Some inventories omitted required elements such as the AI life cycle stage or whether a use case was releasable, and two inventories included AI uses that the agencies later determined were not AI at all. GAO's conclusion is that without accurate inventories, the government's management of its own use of AI will be hindered by incomplete and inaccurate data.

On compliance, GAO reported that 10 of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. Commerce and the General Services Administration fully implemented selected requirements, with Commerce creating a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA establishing an AI Center of Excellence. The Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, the Office of Personnel Management had not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work, and the Office of Science and Technology Policy did not communicate its designation of which agencies were expected to fulfill specific AI requirements. GAO notes there is no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, and that the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. The uses GAO describes are operational and analytical: analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers, identifying information security threats, and facilitating review of large datasets.

The regulatory picture is being written mostly at the state level. The AI Laws section of this site tracks 6,000 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database, and its own summary of that section cites 2,425 bills. From the enrolled text of measures states have passed, the site compared 101 measures across 27 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026, and found that no two states wrote the same law. Only two states passed a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors, Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149, while every other measure names a single setting such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom, or a state agency. No state in that set created a new agency to enforce AI law; the attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively, and several states simply declare a violation to be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act, while insurance commissioners, licensing boards, and election agencies handle their own sectors.

The recurring substantive rule the site identifies is that AI may assist but may not be the only decider where stakes are personal. Insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone under AL SB63 and IA HF2635, AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician under IL HB1806, TN HB1470, and CA AB489, it cannot be the sole instructor of a college course or score a teacher evaluation under IL HB1859 and IL SB2909, and New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions under NY S07599. On the international side, OECD.AI describes itself as helping countries shape trustworthy AI with the OECD AI Principles and gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives, and in July 2024 the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI joined forces under the GPAI brand to create an integrated partnership. Oxford Insights, which produces the Government AI Readiness Index scoring nearly every country on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption, frames its work as helping governments increase the impact of public services by empowering teams and harnessing technology.

Stanford HAI's AI Index, which carries the government and policy track including legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement, reports a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, with technical capabilities improving, investment accelerating, and adoption spreading while the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology fall behind, and it notes that data transparency in the field is declining. For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to a few practical conclusions rather than a return calculation. The sources here report no ROI figures for government AI, so cost-benefit claims would have to come from elsewhere. What the law-tracking material does support is building to the common core: tell people when they are dealing with AI, keep a qualified person in any decision about health, employment, benefits, or education, have a crisis protocol and know the age of your user if your product holds a conversation, and keep records of what the system does, because the attorney general is the enforcer you are most likely to meet. GAO's findings add the internal counterpart, that an agency cannot manage what its own inventory does not accurately describe.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI is a policy observatory that maintains a database of over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, alongside live AI data and policy analysis. The platform promotes the OECD AI Principles to help countries develop trustworthy AI systems, and invites organisations developing advanced AI to submit reports on their risk mitigation measures to improve transparency and comparability. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative merged with OECD member countries' AI work under the GPAI brand to form an integrated partnership. The observatory aims to support AI actors in building systems that respect human rights, fairness, transparency, explainability, robustness, and security.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page reports tracking 5,989 artificial intelligence bills across 53 US jurisdictions, with data refreshed daily from LegiScan. A review of 101 enacted measures across 27 states, dated September 18, 2026, found that no two states wrote the same law. Only Colorado and Texas passed broad laws covering consequential decisions across sectors, while other measures target specific settings such as companion chatbots, political ads, or insurance prior authorizations. The page identifies recurring rules, including that AI may assist but not be the only decider in personal matters like insurance denials or therapy, and that no state created a new enforcement agency; attorneys general typically enforce the larger laws.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
